question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+2 \cdot \left(x+4\right) \cdot y=3 \cdot \left(x+4\right) \cdot y^{2}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+4\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=2 \cdot \left(x+4\right)\\ q(x)&=3 \cdot \left(x+4\right)\\ n&=2.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(- 2 \cdot \left(x+4\right)\right)z=- 3 \cdot \left(x+4\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int - 2 \cdot \left(x+4\right)\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- \left(x+4\right)^{2}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- \left(x+4\right)^{2}}\,z\right)=- 3 \cdot \left(x+4\right) \cdot e^{- \left(x+4\right)^{2}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- \left(x+4\right)^{2}}z=\frac{3 \cdot e^{- \left(x+4\right)^{2}}}{2}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{\left(x+4\right)^{2}} + \frac{3}{2}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{2}{2 \cdot C \cdot e^{\left(x+4\right)^{2}} + 3}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

generation.domains: nonzero real solutions; explicit positive-coordinate and positive-z conditions where needed

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- 2 \cdot y=\sqrt{y}.
$$ Take $y>0$. For even powers and powers of $2/3$ in the choices, retain only intervals where the base is positive. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=-2\\ q(x)&=1\\ n&=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and set $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{2 \cdot \sqrt{y}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-1\right)z=\frac{1}{2}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -1\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- x}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- x}\,z\right)=\frac{e^{- x}}{2}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- x}z=- \frac{e^{- x}}{2}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{x} - \frac{1}{2}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\left(C \cdot e^{x} - \frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. The displayed expression for $z$ must be positive because $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}>0$.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- \frac{2 \cdot y}{\left(x+2\right)}=2 \cdot \sqrt{\left(x+2\right)} \cdot y^{2}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+2\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=- \frac{2}{\left(x+2\right)}\\ q(x)&=2 \cdot \sqrt{\left(x+2\right)}\\ n&=2.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(\frac{2}{\left(x+2\right)}\right)z=- 2 \cdot \sqrt{\left(x+2\right)}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int \frac{2}{\left(x+2\right)}\,\mathrm{d}x}=\left(x+2\right)^{2}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\left(x+2\right)^{2}\,z\right)=- 2 \cdot \left(x+2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$\left(x+2\right)^{2}z=- \frac{4 \cdot \left(x+2\right)^{\frac{7}{2}}}{7}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=\frac{C}{\left(x+2\right)^{2}} - \frac{4 \cdot \left(x+2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{7}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{7 \cdot \left(x+2\right)^{2}}{7 \cdot C - 4 \cdot \left(x+2\right)^{\frac{7}{2}}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+3 \cdot y=3 \cdot \left(x+5\right) \cdot y^{3}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+5\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=3\\ q(x)&=3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)\\ n&=3.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{3}$ and set $z=y^{-2}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-6\right)z=- 6 \cdot \left(x+5\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -6\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}\,z\right)=- 6 \cdot \left(x+5\right) \cdot e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}z=\left(\left(x+5\right) + \frac{1}{6}\right) \cdot e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x+5\right)}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{6 \cdot \left(x+5\right)} + \left(x+5\right) + \frac{1}{6}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-2}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\pm\sqrt{\frac{6}{6 \cdot C \cdot e^{6 \cdot \left(x+5\right)} + 6 \cdot \left(x+5\right) + 1}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. Both signs are retained wherever the radicand is positive.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+2 \cdot y=2 \cdot \left(x-6\right) \cdot y^{3}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x-6\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=2\\ q(x)&=2 \cdot \left(x-6\right)\\ n&=3.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{3}$ and set $z=y^{-2}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-4\right)z=- 4 \cdot \left(x-6\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -4\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 4 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 4 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}\,z\right)=- 4 \cdot \left(x-6\right) \cdot e^{- 4 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 4 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}z=\left(\left(x-6\right) + \frac{1}{4}\right) \cdot e^{- 4 \cdot \left(x-6\right)}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{4 \cdot \left(x-6\right)} + \left(x-6\right) + \frac{1}{4}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-2}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\pm\sqrt{\frac{4}{4 \cdot C \cdot e^{4 \cdot \left(x-6\right)} + 4 \cdot \left(x-6\right) + 1}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. Both signs are retained wherever the radicand is positive.
